The effect of a turn without Cairn stays unmeasured, and the page claims nothing that depends on it. No new delivery, operator input form, model-strategy key, or README row is added. open-question.question: From its clone an agent can read the benchmark checkout, whose inputs area holds the hidden-requirement statements, the sibling clones in the shared scratch directory, and other runs' session transcripts under the host's projects directory, and the maintainer's notes record that Docker Desktop blocks these runs on the development machine. What confinement keeps a run from reading the benchmark checkout, other clones, and other runs' transcripts, and on what machine do runs then execute?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: An operating-system boundary on the existing machine keeps the inputs area and the maintainer's home unreadable to every run with no container runtime, and with runs sequential and per-run cleanup no sibling clone or earlier transcript exists to read; the Mac container option rests on an untested premise about the Docker blocker.
open-question.alternative: Confinement: operating-system file permissions on the development Mac. Every invocation runs as a dedicated unprivileged benchmark user; the benchmark checkout and the maintainer's home are unreadable to it, each clone is created owned by that user with no group or other access, and the user's own home holds its own host configuration and projects directory. Isolation between runs relies on that user's state per run: other clones and earlier transcripts are moved out of its reach or deleted before the next invocation. No container and no second machine. A real OS-enforced boundary for the benchmark checkout and the hidden requirements, independent of the program under test, on the machine the maintainer already has and without touching Docker. All runs share one user, so keeping one run from reading another's clone or transcript depends on per-run cleanup and on runs not overlapping, which ties it to the concurrent-runs sibling; the harness needs privilege escalation to switch users, and the user's tools, browsers, and credentials must be provisioned separately on a machine that also does daily work.

Confinement: none. Runs keep executing as the maintainer's own user on the development Mac, as the draft's "One run" now describes, with no audit of what a session read. The draft rejects the gap with its reason stated: it names the benchmark checkout, the sibling clones under the shared scratch directory, and the host's projects directory as readable from a clone, and records this as a known threat to validity in "Repository layout and isolation". It may say whether the rejection is permanent or deferred to the benchmark repository's implementation. Costs nothing and needs no machine, runtime, or tooling that has not been tested; the draft stays implementable on the maintainer's Mac exactly as written, and the threat is at least disclosed rather than hidden. A run can read the hidden-requirement statements in the inputs area or another scenario's finished clone and nothing would show it, so the hidden axis and every cross-scenario difference rest on the agent not looking, against the draft's own rule that blindness and isolation are properties of what each party is handed, not of discipline.

Confinement: none at run time; runs execute as the maintainer's user on the development Mac. Enforcement is after the fact: once each invocation ends, the harness reads that session's transcript (every tool call with its path and command) and checks it against an allowed set, the clone and the plugin checkout; any read, glob, grep, or shell command touching the benchmark checkout, another clone, or the projects directory voids the run, which is recorded with the reason and excluded from scoring, a rule the draft states beside the pre-flight. Works on the existing machine with no sandbox, OS user, or container, so the Docker Desktop situation never matters, and it produces positive evidence for each scored run that it stayed inside its clone. Detection only: a shell command can reach a path indirectly (a variable, a parent-directory walk, a script it wrote), so a clean audit is not proof, and the voiding rule turns contamination into lost runs and their spent tokens; the transcripts it reads sit in the projects directory whose location the host-configuration sibling decides.

Confinement: the coding host's own controls on the development Mac. The harness runs every invocation with the host's sandboxed shell restricted to the clone (plus read-only access to the plugin checkout) and with permission deny rules for the file-reading tools on the benchmark checkout, the scratch directory's other entries, and the projects directory, carried in a settings file the harness passes; the harness keeps a transcript audit as a backstop, since the boundary is enforced by the program under test. No separate user, container, or machine. Closest to the draft as written: one machine, one user, a per-run settings value the harness already owns, and no new infrastructure to describe or maintain. The boundary is enforced by the agent harness being measured, so a gap in its sandbox or rule matching is a gap in the benchmark; the maintainer's notes record that a shell-granting sandboxed run is exactly what Docker Desktop's stock files block on this Mac, so this may not run here at all, and whether deny rules hold under the permission-skipping flag every invocation uses must be checked before the draft relies on it.

Confinement: one fresh container per run on the development Mac, through a container runtime other than Docker Desktop's (or Docker Desktop itself, if a check shows the recorded blocker concerns only the host's own shell sandbox and not a containerized headless invocation). The container mounts only that run's clone read-write and the plugin checkout read-only, has its own home so its projects directory is its own, and is discarded after the run; the harness and the operator stay outside it on the Mac. Each run sees only its clone by construction, so the benchmark checkout, sibling clones, and other runs' transcripts are all out of reach regardless of what the agent tries or how runs overlap, while the campaign stays on the maintainer's own machine. Rests on an untested premise, that the Docker Desktop blocker does not extend to a container runtime on this Mac; the run then executes on a Linux image rather than macOS, so the image becomes an input whose OS, tools, and browsers must be stated (the execution-environment sibling's axis), and the host's credentials must be passed into each container.

Confinement: one fresh container per run, as in the Mac container option (only the clone read-write, the plugin checkout read-only, a container-own home and projects directory, discarded after the run), executed on a dedicated Linux machine or Linux VM rather than the development Mac. The harness, the benchmark checkout, and the operator run on that host outside the containers; the Mac only starts campaigns and reads results. Strong per-run isolation on a platform where the container and shell-sandbox tooling is known to work, sidestepping the Docker Desktop blocker entirely and leaving the maintainer's machine and configuration out of every run. Needs a Linux machine to be provisioned, paid for or maintained, and kept as a stated environment for the whole campaign, plus the host's credentials on it; nothing in the project has run there yet, so the draft commits to infrastructure that exists only on paper.

Confinement: a whole virtual machine per run. The harness, kept on a controller (the Mac or a server), creates a fresh VM (a cloud instance or a hosted CI runner job) holding only the run's clone, the plugin checkout, and the host binary, drives every invocation in it remotely, collects the outputs and the branch, and destroys the VM; the benchmark checkout and the operator never exist on the run's machine. The strongest boundary on offer: nothing of the benchmark, other runs, or any shared configuration is present on the machine where the agent works, and each run's environment starts from the same image, which also helps reproducibility on another machine. The most infrastructure and the slowest per run: image building, remote control, credential handling per VM, and per-run machine cost, all of it a harness the draft must specify before a single run; a hosted CI runner also ties execution to that service's limits and images.

open-question.question: Nothing states what OS, tools on PATH, and browsers a run finds, though these shape what every scenario can build and what the rater can drive. Is the execution environment declared as a versioned shared input of a comparison set, recorded in the manifest only, or left unrecorded?
open-question.recommendation: The environment shapes what every scenario can build, so it follows the rule every other result-shaping input already follows: declared by content, probed at pre-flight, and a change starting a new set, giving a re-run elsewhere a target instead of a guess.
open-question.alternative: The run environment (OS and version, the tools on PATH with their versions, the installed browsers) is written as one environment definition under the inputs area, versioned by content under an id like the operator definition, and listed among the shared inputs; the pre-flight probes the live machine and refuses the run when it does not match the definition, the manifest records the definition's id, and a change to the definition starts a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing beyond what the seed's CLAUDE.md already says, and the rater's browser stays in the rater definition as now. Puts the environment under the same rule as every other input that shapes results (byte-identical across scenarios, recorded by content, a change never mixed into a comparison), and gives a later re-run on another machine a target it can be checked against rather than a guess. Every probed version has to be held still for a whole campaign, so auto-updating browsers and tools must be pinned or disabled and a drifted machine refuses runs until reprovisioned; whether the pin can be enforced depends on the machine and confinement the filesystem-reach question settles, and whether a change starts a new set rests on the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

The environment is declared inside the seed's CLAUDE.md, which the draft already calls an environment description: it names the OS, the tools on PATH, and the browsers a run finds, so the seed tag versions the declaration and no separate input or manifest field is added; the pre-flight probes the machine against the same list and refuses on a mismatch, and a change to the environment is a change to the seed and starts a new comparison set through the seed tag. The run agent reads the declaration; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Adds no new kind of input and no new versioning path, and every scenario learns equally what it can use (for example that no package manager is present), so no run spends turns discovering the machine or builds against a tool that is absent. Any environment change, even a browser patch release, bumps the seed tag, which invalidates every phase-1 run as a parent for phase 2 and moves the trend's seed line; and telling the agent which tools exist shapes what each scenario builds, turning a measurement condition into part of the prompt every run reads.

The environment is declared as an environment definition under the inputs area, as a provisioning target rather than a set-defining input; the harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records the observed OS, PATH tool versions, and browsers in an environment field of the manifest beside the definition's id, and a mismatch with the definition is flagged by the analysis step and reported beside the affected rows rather than refusing the run or starting a new comparison set. The run agent is told nothing new; the rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Gives another machine a stated target to reproduce while letting a campaign that spans days absorb a browser or tool auto-update without discarding the set, with every deviation visible in the record instead of hidden. A flagged mismatch still sits inside one comparison, so a difference between scenarios can be partly the environment's, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions; the analysis must decide per flag whether it matters, which is a judgment the rest of the design avoids. Whether drift may stay inside a set is the axis the comparison-set-definition question owns.

No environment is declared. The harness probes the live machine at the manifest step and records what it finds (OS and version, a fixed list of tools on PATH with their versions, installed browsers) in an environment field of each run's manifest; the environment is not a shared input, a change starts no new comparison set, and the analysis may group or compare runs by the recorded values after the fact. The rater's browser stays in the rater definition. Costs one probe and one manifest field, needs no provisioning or pinning, and still leaves a record from which any later question about what a run found can be answered. Records without controlling: runs on two machines or across an update mix silently within a set unless someone reads the field, a later re-run has nothing to reproduce but a list of observed versions, and the fixed probe list misses any tool a run reached that the list did not name.

The environment is neither declared nor recorded: a run finds whatever the machine running the harness has, and the draft states this choice with its reason (all scenarios of a campaign run on one machine, so the environment is common to them) instead of leaving it unsaid. Nothing to build, pin, or maintain, and within one campaign on one unchanged machine every scenario does meet the same environment. Results cannot be reproduced or audited elsewhere, and a tool or browser update during a campaign, or a move to another machine (which the filesystem-reach question may require), changes what scenarios can build with no trace, mixed into the trend as if it were a plugin change.

open-question.question: A Cairn skill that stops on its own precondition prints a message and exits 0, so the harness, which stops the chain only on a non-zero exit, carries on past it and can record a chain that closed an empty milestone as every invocation made. By what signal does the harness detect that an invocation stopped on a skill's own check rather than completing?
open-question.recommendation: Cairn already ends every successful chain invocation on a fixed identifier-free line, so an allowlist catches every stop including ones no list anticipated, ends the chain so the pointer stays on milestone 1 as the phase-2 text assumes, and with fixed stop lines the recorded first stopping line names which stop it was.
open-question.alternative: Signal: the final message of each cairn chain invocation (the `result` of its JSON output, after any replies) is matched against the delivery's per-line list of expected lines, the skill's fixed success line plus any no-op line whose wording is fixed (today only the bootstrap's `Workflow already bootstrapped — nothing changed.`), and a message carrying none of them counts as a stop. Consequence: a detected stop ends the chain exactly as a non-zero exit does, and the manifest records the first stopping line (for example `invocations.first_stop`) with `made` counting the invocations actually run. Needs no change to Cairn. Works on Cairn as it ships today, because every chain skill already ends a successful run on one fixed identifier-free line, and an allowlist catches every kind of stop, including one no list anticipated, so the empty-milestone chain of gap 5 halts at the derive line and the pointer still names milestone 1 as the phase-2 text assumes. Any final message without a listed line counts as a stop, so a legitimate no-op whose wording is only exemplified (a recommendation pass with nothing to write, a task run that committed nothing) or a model that paraphrases its success line halts a healthy chain, and the list must be kept in step with each Cairn version a delivery names; how many no-op lines can be listed depends on the fixed-stop-line-wording axis.

Signal: the same per-line match of the final message against the expected success and fixed no-op lines as in Expected success line. Consequence: a detected stop is recorded (the first stopping line in the manifest, `made` still counting every invocation the list ran) but does not end the chain; every planned line still runs, and only a non-zero exit stops it. Needs no change to Cairn. Keeps the chain behaving exactly as a headless user's `claude -p` chain does, which also continues past a skill that stopped on exit 0, so the run measures Cairn as it is used while the manifest no longer reads a stopped chain as complete, and a misclassified no-op costs a wrong record line rather than a truncated run. The lines after a stop still run against the state it left, so a refused derivation still reaches the finish line and closes an empty milestone, clearing the pointer the phase-2 text expects to still name milestone 1; the record is corrected but the artifact and the phase-2 starting point are not.

Signal: the final message is matched against each skill's own fixed precondition-stop and no-op lines, and a message carrying a stop line counts as a stop, identified by which line matched; any other message is taken as completion. Consequence: a detected stop ends the chain as a non-zero exit does, and the manifest records the first stopping line together with the stop it hit. Relies on Cairn fixing the wording of every stop line. Names which check stopped the chain, not only that one did, so the record says "derivation refused on open questions" rather than "something other than success", and a model that paraphrases its success line is never mistaken for a stop. Viable only where every chain skill's stop lines carry fixed wording, which is the fixed-stop-line-wording axis, and a denylist misses any stop it does not list (a new check in a later Cairn version, a model that rephrases a stop), letting that chain run on exactly as it does today.

Signal: after each cairn invocation the harness inspects the clone instead of the message: the delivery declares per line the commit subject marker the skill writes on success (`Milestone-activation:`, `Task-derivation:`, `Milestone-finish:`, and so on) or a state test (the pointer names a milestone, `TASKS_TODO.md` holds a section), and an invocation that added no such commit and failed its test counts as a stop. Consequence: a detected stop ends the chain as a non-zero exit does, and the manifest records the first stopping line. Needs no change to Cairn. Reads what the skill actually did rather than what the model said, resting on Cairn's invariant that every file-changing skill commits its own paths under a fixed marker, so paraphrase and message wording never matter and the signal is reproducible from the run branch alone. A pass that legitimately changed nothing (a recommendation pass with nothing to write, a review pass that found nothing, the bootstrap at phase 2) commits nothing exactly like a pass that stopped, so each line's no-op case needs its own state test or is ambiguous, and the per-line table of markers and tests is a second description of each skill's behaviour that must be kept in step with every Cairn version a delivery names.

Signal: the model call that already reads each final message for the reactive-turn decision also returns a stop verdict, stop or completion, from the message's content, with no list of lines. Consequence: a stop verdict ends the chain as a non-zero exit does, and the verdict is written into the operator record and the manifest's first stopping line. Needs no change to Cairn. Handles any wording, paraphrased success lines and unfixed no-op lines included, with no per-version list to maintain, and adds no step beyond the reading of each final message the harness already makes. Makes whether a chain continued a model judgment that can differ between two runs of the same message, so a chain's length becomes partly attributable to the classifier rather than the scenario, and it widens the operator's role from a stakeholder stand-in to a harness judge; how the final-message reading is made and recorded is the reply-need-classification axis.

Signal: none beyond the process exit code; a skill's own stop is not detected and the chain runs on past it as today. The draft instead stops claiming otherwise: `made` over `planned` is redefined as invocations run rather than how far the chain got, the phase-2 text no longer assumes a stopped chain leaves the pointer on milestone 1, and where a chain stopped is read by hand from the invocation outputs, as the draft already does for every other part of the record. Adds no matching rule, table, or classifier to build and keep in step with Cairn, and keeps the run identical to an unattended user's chain, consistent with the draft's position that the record is read case by case and never turned into a metric. A chain that closed an empty milestone still reads as every invocation made, so the manifest and any summary drawn from it cannot tell a completed chain from one that stopped at derivation, and the empty-milestone outcome is avoided only to the extent the finish skill itself refuses it, which is the finish-with-no-tasks axis.

open-question.question: No scenario invocation carries a time or turn limit while the rater has one, so a runaway session can hold a run open indefinitely. Does each invocation get a time or turn limit, and how is an invocation that hits it classified?
open-question.alternative: Two generous limits per claude -p process, both declared as shared inputs of the comparison set. The first is a host-enforced spend or turn cap; reaching it is a behavioural early stop, recorded and rated on the tree left. The second is a harness wall-clock ceiling set above anything the spend cap allows in normal operation; a kill there is classified as an infrastructure failure and handled by the infrastructure-failure policy. The manifest records which limit ended the invocation. Sorts the two ways a session runs away by mechanism, not by judgment: a model that keeps working hits the spend cap and is scored, and a session that stalls hits the clock and is not. This bounds every run without scoring outside slowdowns against a scenario. Two parameters to set, declare, and justify instead of one, plus a dependence on a host flag whose coverage of subagents must be confirmed. Handling of the clock hit depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

Scenario invocations keep running with no time, turn, or spend limit, per invocation or per run, as the draft's one-run procedure now stands. A session ends only by itself or by a failed call, its wall-clock duration is recorded in the manifest as today, and no limit-hit end class exists. Adds no parameter to the design and cuts no scenario short. A slow invocation, most likely Cairn's long task-completion line, can never be stopped by a ceiling set too low, so no score depends on where the ceiling was set. A runaway or hung session holds its run, and any campaign waiting behind it, open indefinitely. The only way to end it is a person killing the process, which breaks the draft's rule that nothing about a run is done by hand, and the kill leaves an end that no rule classifies.

The harness kills each claude -p process after a fixed wall-clock ceiling. This covers the first-form invocation and each operator-reply resume, each process timed on its own. The ceiling is set generously, well above the longest normal invocation (for example a stated multiple of a pilot's longest), and declared as a shared input of the comparison set. A kill stops the chain and is recorded in the manifest as its own end class (time limit). The run is then scored like any other early stop: a result, rated on the tree it left. Bounds every run with one harness-side mechanism that needs no host flag and catches hangs as well as loops. It rarely binds, so it does not shape scores, and it fits the draft's existing rule that an early stop is a result, not a failed measurement. Wall-clock time also depends on API speed and the network, so a hit can come from a stalled connection rather than the model, and counting it as a result scores an outside slowdown against the scenario. Cairn's long invocations are the most exposed to this.

The same generous per-process wall-clock ceiling, declared as a shared input of the comparison set and enforced by the harness, but a kill is classified as an infrastructure failure, not a behavioural stop. It is recorded under that end class and handled by whatever the benchmark does with infrastructure failures, so it is not scored as the scenario's result. A scenario is not penalised for a session held open by something outside the model, such as a stalled API or network. That keeps the bias the gaps report raises (Cairn, the heaviest spender, being the likeliest to hit external limits) out of the scores. A genuine model runaway, such as a loop that never converges, also gets treated as an infrastructure failure, which hides a real behavioural failure mode and can reward it with a retry. What a hit costs depends on the axis the infrastructure-failure question owns.

alternative.id: Spend or turn cap as result

open-question.alternative: Each invocation runs under a fixed cap the host enforces in the model's own terms: a dollar budget (claude -p's --max-budget-usd) or a cap on agentic turns where the host offers one. The cap is set generously and declared as a shared input of the comparison set, and there is no wall-clock ceiling. Reaching the cap is a behavioural early stop, recorded in the manifest under a limit end class and rated on the tree left. A cap counted in spend or turns does not depend on API or network speed, so a hit always reflects what the model did. Classifying it as a result is then sound. It is also one parameter that is easy to state and to reproduce. It does not bound a hang that spends nothing, such as a stalled connection or a blocked tool call, so the indefinitely-open run the question raises remains possible. It also depends on a host flag whose scope over dispatched subagents must be confirmed, and that flag is recorded per host rather than enforced by the harness.

A deliberately tight per-invocation limit, in time or spend, that is the same for every scenario and chosen to bind rather than to catch only runaways. Reaching it is an early stop rated on the tree left, so the benchmark measures quality reached within a fixed resource budget. Answers the question of which approach does best when given the same resources, a comparison a reader can take at face value without weighing cost separately. Turns the cost the draft reports beside quality into a constraint on quality. The draft states that Cairn is expected to cost more and that the benchmark reports by how much, so this would systematically cut Cairn's heaviest lines short and score that against it, and the scores would then depend on where the budget was set.

A single wall-clock ceiling on the whole run (every invocation, reply, and operator turn of one prompt's chain), declared as a shared input of the comparison set, with no per-invocation limit. When the deadline passes the harness kills the running process and stops the chain. The run is recorded with a deadline end class and rated on the tree left as an early stop. One number bounds every run's total duration, and with it the length of a campaign, without having to size a ceiling for each kind of invocation. Chains differ greatly in length, from the single manual message to Cairn's eleven or more lines, so one deadline either binds Cairn or is slack for manual. It also lets a runaway early invocation use up the time of every later line, so the stop shows up at a line that did nothing wrong.

open-question.question: A new rating writes new browser tests for every checklist line, so two ratings of one artifact can test the same line at different strictness, and the draft's claim that a second rating gets the same number holds only for re-running an existing test. What must a rater version pass before it may rate a comparison set, and what is the acceptance rule?
open-question.recommendation: A reference artifact with variants each built to fail known lines catches exactly the weak-test failure the question names with a rule that has one answer and no judgment, and with every line carrying a case-and-assertion spec an exact pass is reachable.
open-question.alternative: A calibration set per prompt version is a shared input: one reference artifact that meets every checklist line, plus deliberately broken variants, each built to fail a known set of lines, so that every test line is failed by at least one variant. Each reading line gets reference items whose verdicts are clear-cut. Every artifact has a recorded verdict for every line. The set is frozen beside the checklist version a comparison set uses. Before it may rate that set, a rater version rates every calibration artifact once through the normal rating path, writing fresh tests that the harness runs. The acceptance rule is exact: every verdict must match the recorded one, and a not-proved verdict counts as a mismatch. A single mismatch refuses the version, which is changed (guideline, model, effort, or budget) and calibrated again as a new rater version. The calibration ratings and their tests are committed as the version's evidence. It catches the failure the question names: a weak test passes on the variant built to fail it, so a rater that tests the same line too leniently cannot rate anything. The rule has one answer and needs no judgment, like every other check in the design. Building a correct reference and enough broken variants for every line of both prompts is substantial work that must be redone whenever a checklist changes. One pass shows that the version can be accurate, not that two fresh ratings agree. A rule with zero tolerance may never be met by a model writing new tests, which would stall every comparison set. How reachable it is depends on whether checklist lines carry test specifications, an axis a sibling question owns.

No calibration gate: a rater version may rate a comparison set as soon as it is defined, with no reference artifacts and no acceptance rule. The draft drops "a second rating of the same artifact gets the same number" and states only what holds, that re-running a rating's committed tests reproduces its verdicts, and leaves the variation between fresh ratings to whatever the sibling questions on repeat-rating agreement and per-line test specifications settle. This is meant as never, not later. No reference artifacts to build or keep in step with each prompt version, and no extra rater runs, so the design stays as small as it is now and stops claiming a property it has not measured. A rater version that writes weak tests (an undo button exists rather than the award being reversed) is caught by nothing before its verdicts reach the published scores, and its strictness differs between rater versions with no shared yardstick. How much noise is left depends on the repeat-rating and line-specification axes the sibling questions own.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with a known verdict on every line and a not-proved verdict counted as a mismatch. Before it may rate a comparison set, a rater version rates every calibration artifact a declared number of times (more than one, for example three), each time as an independent rating with fresh tests. The acceptance rule is exact on every repetition: every verdict of every rating matches the recorded one. Any mismatch refuses the version. All repetitions and their tests are committed as evidence. It tests the claim the draft makes, that a second fresh rating gets the same number, against known answers before any score depends on it. It catches both a lenient test and one that is strict in some ratings and lenient in others, which a single pass can miss. The calibration cost is multiplied by the repetition count, and a zero-tolerance rule over several independent ratings is the hardest of all to meet, so a merely good rater version is the most likely to be refused here. It also builds and maintains the whole reference and variant set. Its reachability depends on the line-specification axis a sibling question owns.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with known verdicts on every line. A rater version rates it a declared number of times (one or more) and passes when its agreement with the recorded verdicts reaches a minimum the draft states, for example per axis, with a not-proved verdict counted as a disagreement. Below the minimum the version is refused. A version that passes publishes its agreement figures and every mismatched line beside the comparison set's results. It is a gate that a capable model writing fresh tests can actually pass, while still stopping a rater version that is clearly too lenient or too erratic. Publishing the mismatches shows a reader how much of a score's line count to trust. The tolerated mismatch rate is rater noise that enters every published score and the lost count. The threshold is a number the design has no principled source for. It still carries the cost of building and maintaining the reference and variant set.

The same frozen calibration set per prompt version, with known verdicts on every line, rated by each rater version a declared number of times before or alongside a comparison set. No acceptance rule refuses the version. Its agreement with the recorded verdicts, and the lines it got wrong, are reported beside the comparison set's scores the way the not-proved count is. No comparison set is ever blocked by a rater version that narrowly fails, yet every reader sees how far the rater that produced a score reproduces known verdicts, using the same mechanism the draft already uses for the not-proved count. A demonstrably lenient rater version still produces published scores and ranks, so the reported figure explains noise after the fact rather than keeping it out. The question asks what a rater must pass, and this answers that it passes nothing.

The calibration set is real artifacts from pilot runs of the scenarios rather than purpose-built ones. The maintainer plays each one by hand and records a verdict on every checklist line, and the items and verdicts are frozen as a shared input beside the checklist version. A rater version rates the set before it may rate a comparison set, with a not-proved verdict counted as a mismatch. The acceptance rule is exact. A mismatch is checked by playing the artifact again: if the recorded verdict was wrong, it is corrected as a new calibration-set version; otherwise the rater version is refused. The rater is calibrated on the structural variety real runs produce (multi-file layouts, unusual controls, partial features), which a reference and its variants written by one person do not show. No variants need to be engineered. The known verdicts come from a person's judgment, which the design otherwise keeps out of every number. Lines that no pilot artifact happens to fail have no failing case, so a lenient test on them is never caught. Settling mismatches puts a hand step into the gate.

No known verdicts: the calibration set is a fixed, frozen set of artifacts, such as pilot or earlier-run artifacts. A rater version rates each of them twice, with fresh tests each time, before it may rate a comparison set. The acceptance rule is agreement between its own two ratings, line by line, at a stated minimum or exactly. Below that the version is refused. Nothing needs a reference artifact, broken variants, or hand verdicts, so it is the cheapest gate to set up and keep current across prompt versions. It measures the instability between fresh ratings that the draft's "same number" claim leaves unmeasured. Two ratings that are equally lenient agree perfectly, so the weak-test failure the question opens with passes the gate unseen. It also partly overlaps the repeat-rating agreement on comparison-set artifacts, which a sibling question owns.

open-question.question: The published trend follows per-scenario aggregates across comparison sets and plugin commits, so a change to the inputs and a change to the plugin are mixed in one line, against the rule that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions. How does the trend continue when a shared input changes?
open-question.recommendation: Every segment obeys the attribution rule at no cost beyond the runs the release gate and development loop already make, and since the gate runs the previous release under the candidate's inputs each segment starts with at least that pair; back-catalogue re-runs would grow without bound.
open-question.alternative: Nothing is re-run when a shared input changes. The trend restarts as a new segment under the new comparison set and grows only as later commits are benchmarked under it. Each segment is drawn on its own, with the input change that opened it labeled at the boundary, and no line crosses from one segment to the next. The release gate already runs the previous release under the candidate's inputs, so a new segment starts with at least that pair. It needs no runs beyond those the release gate and the development loop already make, and every segment still obeys the attribution rule, because a line never joins points taken under different inputs. Each input change throws away the trend's history. If inputs change about as often as releases ship, segments stay two or three points long and the trend says little more than the release-gate comparison. How often that happens depends on the comparison-set definition a sibling owns.

The trend is kept within one comparison set. When a shared input changes, every plugin commit already on the trend is re-run under the new set, so every point on the published line shares the same seed, prompts, operator, and every other shared input, and a step between two points can only come from the plugin. The previous set's trend is kept as an archived record and is never joined to the new one. This is the gaps report's proposed fix (gap 12). Every difference along the line comes from the plugin commit alone, which fully meets the draft's attribution rule (":7", ":11"), and the trend always shows the full release history under the current inputs, the best ones the benchmark has. Each input change costs a full chain and a rater run for every release on the trend, times the runs each scenario needs, and that cost keeps growing as releases accumulate. Old commits may no longer run under a newer host CLI or model, and then they drop off the line anyway. How often this cost comes due depends on which versions define a comparison set, which a sibling question owns; a set keyed to an auto-updating CLI would trigger it often. Which scenarios each re-run covers depends on the roster, which another sibling owns.

When a shared input changes, a fixed number of the most recent releases (stated in the draft, for example the last two or three) is re-run under the new set. A new trend segment starts at the oldest re-run release. Older points stay in the previous segment, drawn as a separate line with the input change marked at the break, and no line ever crosses a segment boundary. Each segment stays fully attributable to the plugin, the re-run cost of each input change is bounded no matter how many releases exist, and the recent history most relevant to current development carries over into the new segment. The long-range trend falls into segments that cannot be compared with each other, so the trend cannot show cumulative progress beyond the window. The window size is a judgment call the draft has to defend. The cost per input change is still several releases' worth of runs, and it comes due as often as the comparison-set definition, owned by a sibling, starts a new set.

When a shared input changes, one anchor release (the latest on the trend) is re-run under the new set. The new segment is then shifted by the anchor's score difference between the old and new sets, so the published trend stays one continuous line. The splice point and the estimated input effect are stated on the line. It keeps one continuous long-range trend for the cost of a single release's re-run per input change, and unlike an unmarked join it measures the input effect and reports it instead of folding it silently into the plugin's line. The splice assumes an input change shifts every commit's score by the same amount, which a new prompt, rater, or operator has no reason to do. Errors from successive splices add up along the line, and the anchor's shift is itself a difference of two noisy scores, as reliable as the runs per scenario a sibling question sets. The line therefore still mixes input and plugin effects, only less visibly, which goes against the attribution rule.

The trend gets its own comparison set whose shared inputs are pinned and never revised. Every release is benchmarked under that frozen set for the trend, alongside whatever newer set drives the README page's ranking and radar. Input revisions go only into the newer sets. A segment break happens only when a frozen input can no longer be run at all, for example a retired model. Every point on the trend shares identical inputs for as long as they stay runnable, with no back-catalogue re-runs, so the line is both continuous and fully attributable to the plugin. Every release pays for a second campaign on the frozen set, and the trend keeps measuring against inputs the benchmark has already found worth fixing (a corrected prompt, a calibrated rater), so it can disagree with the current page. Model retirement and host CLI updates force breaks anyway. Whether the CLI can be pinned at all depends on the comparison-set definition a sibling owns.

The trend stays as the draft has it: per-scenario aggregates followed across comparison sets and plugin commits as one line. Each input change is marked on the line with what changed, and the draft states that the trend is a descriptive history that attributes nothing, carving it out of the attribution rule. It costs no runs and no new machinery, and it keeps the longest unbroken view of how the scores moved over the benchmark's life. A step at an input change cannot be split between plugin and inputs. Cairn's changelog links to the trend for each release, which invites exactly the attribution the carve-out disclaims, and the draft's own statement that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions then has a published exception.

No trend across comparison sets or plugin commits is published. The README page keeps the current set's ranking and radar. Each release's changelog entry links instead to that release's gate comparison, the candidate against the previous release under the same inputs and model strategy. The "Published trend" use is removed from the draft, or deferred as a convention with the reason stated. It removes the confound entirely without adding cost, since the release gate already produces a within-set comparison for every release, which is the attributable form of what a trend would show. The benchmark loses any long-range view of Cairn's progress across releases, so a reader or a grant reviewer can see only pairwise steps and the current standing, not whether the plugin has improved over time.

open-question.question: Each hidden requirement's evidence must settle the question once asked while the prompt alone gives no reason to ask, and nothing has tested this: prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" may already invite the topic question, and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" sits close to the export convention. What procedure and acceptance rule calibrate each prompt's hidden requirement before scored runs?
open-question.recommendation: Each half of the calibration rule gets its own measurement and threshold, so a failure says whether to weaken or strengthen the evidence, where a bare met rate cannot tell asking from inferring; the asked arm's fixed question is the entry's declared bearing scope.
open-question.alternative: A pre-run pilot with two arms per prompt, one for each half of the calibration rule, each run a small fixed number of times under the strongest manual model pair. The unasked arm runs manual_prompt with the operator's hidden knowledge withheld, so every question gets a reply that discloses nothing; it measures whether the prompt and seed lead to the requirement with no disclosure. Its acceptance rule is a met-rate ceiling. The asked arm gives a model the seed tree and the prompt plus one fixed bearing question written by the maintainer (what the questions should be about; where a written set should live), with no operator, and checks whether its answer, grounded in the evidence alone, is the hidden requirement. Its acceptance rule is a hit-rate floor. A requirement passes only when both arms pass. A failed ceiling is fixed by weakening the evidence or the prompt's invitation, and a failed floor by strengthening the evidence, each as a seed bump or prompt revision followed by another pilot. Pilot runs are never scored. Each half of the stated rule (no reason to ask from the prompt alone; one clearly best answer once asked) gets its own measurement and threshold, so a failure says whether to weaken or strengthen the evidence. The asked arm also checks the grounding the YOLO chain depends on when it accepts its own recommendation without the operator. It adds two pilot-only harness modes, an operator with its hidden knowledge stripped and a direct probe call, that no scored delivery uses. The asked arm's result depends on how the maintainer words the bearing question, which assumes the very question a run is supposed to surface. Its operator-withheld arm depends on how the sibling bearing-question test defines a disclosure-triggering question.

A pre-run pilot, the design-gaps report's fix taken as written. For each prompt the draft states a pilot: the bare manual_prompt delivery is run a small fixed number of times (five, say) with the operator as defined, hidden knowledge included, under the comparison set's strongest manual model pair. Prompt 2's pilot runs start from the pilot's own phase-1 runs. The real rater scores the hidden check line. The acceptance rule is one band on the met rate: a requirement met in almost every run has evidence that is too strong, or a prompt that invites the question; one met in no run has evidence that is too faint; a rate between the two passes. A failure is fixed by revising the seed evidence (a seed bump) or the prompt and running the pilot again. Pilot runs belong to no comparison set and are never scored. It is the cheapest procedure that tests anything empirically, and it reuses the delivery, operator, and rater the draft already defines with no pilot-only machinery. The met rate mixes runs that met the requirement because they asked and were told with runs that inferred it unasked. A high rate could mean a model that asks well, not evidence that is too strong, so the band cannot tell which half of the calibration rule failed. A five-run band is also too coarse to separate a 20% rate from a 60% one.

A pre-run pilot of every scenario in the planned roster, manual and Cairn deliveries alike, each run a few times per prompt with the operator as defined and rated by the real rater. The acceptance rule asks whether the hidden axis discriminates: a requirement passes when its met rate is neither at the ceiling nor at the floor across all scenarios together. When every scenario meets it, the evidence is too strong; when none does, too faint. A failure is fixed by revising the evidence or the prompt and running the pilot again. Pilot runs are excluded from every comparison set. It tests the axis for what it is meant to do, separating deliveries, under the exact conditions the scored runs will have, including Cairn's review and recommendation path, which a manual-only pilot never exercises. It costs about as much as a small comparison set. Tuning the evidence until the scenarios spread also tunes it against the deliveries being compared, which invites calibrating toward the Cairn margin the benchmark exists to test. Its scope depends on the roster the sibling scenario-roster question defines.

No pilot runs. The draft states an authoring checklist that each hidden requirement and its evidence must pass before the requirement is used. The evidence names neither the requirement nor its key word. The requirement is no convention of the project's category and appears on no implied-requirement or left-open list. The prompt contains no phrase that points at the bearing question (prompt 1's "ten questions of its own" and prompt 2's "keep them for the next party" are reviewed against this). The answer follows from the evidence only once the question is asked. The maintainer and one independent reader both judge each item, and the acceptance rule is that every item passes for both readers. A failure is fixed by rewording the evidence or the prompt before the inputs are used. It costs no runs and can be settled entirely in the draft, and it catches the two concerns the question names (the prompt's own invitation, and prompt 2's closeness to an export convention) as reviewable wording problems. It replaces the test the gap says is missing with the same kind of judgment that produced the untested evidence. Whether a model makes the zoo-to-animals inference unasked, or exports a set by habit, is empirical, and a reader's verdict on it can be wrong in either direction without anything showing it.

No separate pilot before scored runs. Calibration is checked once, after the first comparison set has been rated, by reading the operator records and ratings already kept. For each prompt the audit counts the runs that met the hidden requirement with no bearing question in the operator record (inferred unasked) and the runs that failed it although the statement was disclosed or the evidence was present. The acceptance rule is a ceiling on the first count and a ceiling on the second, stated in the draft. Until the audit passes, that set's hidden-axis scores are published marked provisional. A failure revises the evidence or the prompt for the next set, as a seed bump or prompt revision. It spends nothing beyond the scored runs, and it calibrates on the full run count and every delivery rather than a handful of pilot runs, so the rates it reads are less noisy than any affordable pilot's. The first set's hidden axis is spent on evidence nobody had tested and is published before calibration is known. The audit also turns the run record into a pass-fail judgment, which the draft has so far kept out of measurement, and it depends on how the sibling bearing-question test decides that a recorded question bore on the requirement.

No pre-run gate. Instead every comparison set carries one control: manual_prompt under the strongest manual model pair, run with the operator's hidden knowledge withheld. Its hidden-requirement met rate is reported beside the hidden axis as the floor that inference alone reaches, so a reader can see how much of each scenario's hidden score asking could have added. The requirement is kept whatever the control shows. The acceptance rule is disclosure only, with no threshold that blocks scored runs, and a revision stays the maintainer's call between sets. Calibration is measured in every set under that set's own models and host version, so the measurement stays current as models learn to infer more, and it never blocks a set or tunes the evidence toward a result. A requirement whose evidence is too strong or too faint keeps being scored, with the problem only disclosed beside it. Each set pays for an extra scenario. Whether the control belongs in a set depends on the roster the sibling scenario-roster question defines.

The empirical calibration requirement is dropped. The draft states no pilot procedure and no acceptance rule. It keeps the calibration bullet as an authoring intent only and says plainly that the evidence has not been tested: prompt 1's wording may invite the topic question, and prompt 2's request sits close to an export convention. The hidden axis is read with that limitation. It costs nothing and adds no procedure to a benchmark that has not been implemented yet, and it is honest about what the design does and does not guarantee. The axis may then measure whether a model read README.md, which the draft itself rules out as a valid hidden requirement, and nothing would ever show whether it does. The milestone goal names the hidden-requirement pilot as a gap to resolve by stated procedure, so this option rejects that gap and must give its reason in the draft.

open-question.question: Each prompt's checklist is derived from the draft's project section, which no version pins, and nothing freezes the checklist and hidden requirements before a comparison set's first scored run. Are the checklist and hidden-requirement entries frozen before the first scored run of a set, and how?
open-question.recommendation: Pre-registers the checklist and hidden entries before any result exists with the harness enforcing it, and matches each correction to its cost: a run-side change the operator reads starts a new set, a rating-side line re-rates immutable snapshots.
open-question.alternative: The checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area and committed with the hidden-requirement entries before a set's first scored run. Their blob hashes are fixed as frozen versions, and the harness refuses a scored run that does not match them. After the freeze, a changed hidden-requirement statement, which the operator reads, starts a new comparison set with fresh runs. A changed checklist line or hidden check line is issued as a new rating version that re-rates every artifact of the set. The earlier ratings and frozen version are kept, and the analysis never mixes versions. Pre-registers the first version before any result exists, so every later revision is visibly a revision. A correction to rating-side lines costs only a re-rating of the immutable artifacts, not a re-run. Uses two change paths (run-side and rating-side) where one rule would do, and the hidden-requirement entry is split across them. Revisions after results are seen remain possible, and they are visible but not prevented. Its rating-version path has to fit whatever acceptance rule a rater version must pass before it may rate a set.

Nothing is pinned. Each rating derives the checklist from the project section as it stands when the rating runs, and the hidden-requirement entries stay editable at any point. The manifest and rating files record no version of either, and the analysis groups runs only by the inputs it already records (seed tag, prompt blobs). Adds no input, field, or harness check, and a defect found in a checklist line or a hidden entry can be fixed the moment someone sees it. Two ratings in one comparison set can be scored against different checklists with no record of it. Nothing stops a checklist line or hidden check from being reworded after results are seen. This breaks the draft's own rule that every shared input is recorded by content and that a difference is attributed only to what differs between definitions.

The project section the checklist is derived from (per prompt, together with every earlier prompt's section) is recorded by blob hash in each manifest and rating file, and so is each hidden-requirement entry. The checklist itself stays unmaterialized and is re-derived from the pinned section at each rating. There is no gate: an edit is a new version that the analysis groups by. Uses the draft's own versioning idiom (content hashes in the manifest) and the smallest change to the design: no new checklist file and no harness refusal. Pinning the source does not pin the derived lines. A rating agent turning prose into lines can split, merge, or reword them differently on each rating, so the line ids the lost-since-parent count depends on are not stable. Edits after results are seen are recorded but not prevented.

The checklist is materialized as one committed file per prompt in the inputs area, its lines carrying their ids, axes, and kinds. That file and each hidden-requirement entry are recorded by blob hash in every manifest and rating file. There is no gate before the first scored run. A changed hidden-requirement statement, which the operator reads, means fresh runs. A changed checklist or check line means the set's existing artifacts are re-rated against the new version, and the analysis never compares ratings made under different versions. Line ids and wording become a fixed artifact every rating reads, every rating is traceable to the exact lines it used, and a correction is cheap: a re-rating of artifacts that are already immutable snapshots. Nothing prevents tuning the lines or a hidden check after seeing which scenario they favour. The record makes such a change visible in the history but does not stop it, and re-rating under a convenient new version is easy. Whether these hashes become part of a comparison set's identity depends on how a comparison set is defined.

As in Record by content, the checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area, and it and each hidden-requirement entry are recorded by blob hash in every manifest. Both are treated as shared run inputs like the seed and the prompts, so any change to either starts a new comparison set with fresh runs of every scenario. There is still no gate before the first scored run. One uniform rule for every shared input: a change of any of them is a new set. A set never holds artifacts rated against two checklists, and no separate rating-version concept is needed for the checklist. A typo fix in one checklist line costs a full re-run of every scenario, which the immutable artifacts did not need. The first scored runs can still start before the inputs settle, so early sets are likely to be thrown away. This option depends on comparison-set identity including these hashes and on how superseded sets are shown.

The checklist is materialized per prompt in the inputs area and committed with the hidden-requirement entries before a set's first scored run. Their blob hashes are fixed as the set's frozen versions. The harness refuses a scored run, and the rater refuses a rating, whose checklist or hidden entry differs from the frozen versions. Any later change to either starts a new comparison set with fresh runs of every scenario. Gives the strongest guarantee against post-hoc tuning, a pre-registration in effect. Every artifact in a set was produced and rated against inputs fixed before any result existed, and the harness enforces this rather than discipline. Combines the costliest correction (a full re-run for any fix) with a new harness check. The freeze is only as good as the inputs at freeze time, so it has to follow whatever calibration of hidden requirements and rater happens before scored runs. Like Record, new set, it depends on comparison-set identity and on how superseded sets are shown.

open-question.question: Nothing lists which scenarios a comparison set must contain, so "complete" is undefined and the strongest manual strategy can be left out while the radar claims to compare against it. Does a comparison set declare a roster of scenarios that must all be rated before it counts as complete, and what must the roster hold?
open-question.recommendation: A pre-declared roster gives complete an exact meaning and guarantees the headline baseline by construction at the cost of one manual scenario; the minimum holds every primary delivery, the clarify delivery included under the same rule-named pair.
open-question.alternative: A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set, as a file in the inputs area. It must hold at least the following: cairn yolo and cairn assess for the set's Cairn version under the reference strategy models_strategy_1; the multi-prompt mirror of that cairn yolo scenario; and manual_prompt under the single pair named by a stated rule, namely the most capable model the set's pinned host version offers at that model's highest effort level. Further scenarios may be listed on top of this minimum. The radar's claim to compare against the strongest manual configuration is guaranteed by construction at the cost of one manual scenario, and every primary delivery appears in every set. The headline comparison can therefore never be read against a deliberately weak baseline. "Strongest" is assumed, not measured. Highest effort on the top model is not guaranteed to score best on this project, and "most capable" still needs a stated reading when the host offers models that trade one strength for another. Each run multiplies the cost of every mandatory scenario, depending on how many runs a set requires per scenario.

A comparison set declares no roster. "Complete" is defined as every scenario that has at least one run in the set having both phases of each of its runs rated. The radar's claim about "the strongest manual configuration" is narrowed to "the best manual configuration this set ran", and the line under the chart already names the scenario each curve comes from. Adds no new input file and no planning step. The draft's completeness condition and its radar wording become exact about what they promise, and the set stays free to run whatever the maintainer can afford. Omission is still possible. A set can leave out the strongest manual configuration, or every multi-prompt control, and still count as complete, so it is the reader who has to notice from the scenario ids that a stronger manual pair was never run. A set's coverage depends on what happened to be run, not on a rule.

Each comparison set has a roster file in the benchmark's inputs area that lists scenario ids. It is declared before the set's first scored run and not changed during the set. The set is complete once every listed scenario has its runs rated in both phases, and the README page draws only from roster scenarios. No rule constrains what the roster lists. "Complete" gets an exact, pre-declared meaning, and once a set has started it cannot pick its comparison after seeing the scores. All this costs is one short file per set. Nothing stops the roster itself from leaving out the strongest manual configuration, so the radar's fairness claim still rests on the maintainer's judgment at declaration time. How a roster change relates to set identity depends on how the comparison set is defined.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set. It must hold at least the following: cairn yolo and cairn assess under models_strategy_1; the multi-prompt mirror of that cairn yolo scenario; and manual_prompt under every model the set's pinned host version offers, each at its highest effort level. The strongest manual configuration is then whichever of these scores highest, not one named in advance. The strongest manual configuration is found by measurement instead of being assumed, which closes the gap a rule-named pair leaves. It also gives the manual family several configurations, as Cairn has, so a best-of selection is not lopsided between families. Several manual scenarios per set multiply the cost of every set, run counts included. Choosing the best of several manual configurations brings in the best-of-noise selection effect that the radar curve rule has to account for, so how well this option works depends on how each family's curve is selected.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run and fixed for the set, as a matrix rather than a list. It names a set of single-pair model strategies (each model the pinned host offers, at its highest effort) plus Cairn's reference strategy. Every primary delivery runs under every single-pair strategy: manual_prompt, the multi-prompt mirror of each cairn yolo scenario, cairn yolo, and cairn assess. The two cairn deliveries also run under models_strategy_1. The set is complete only when every cell is rated. Every delivery is compared with every other under identical model pairs, so the attribution rule that "two scenarios sharing a strategy isolate the delivery" holds across the whole page. Every family also has the same configurations, which removes the selection asymmetry between Cairn and manual at its source. This is the most expensive roster by far, since cost grows with deliveries times strategies times runs. Most of the cells run Cairn under a single pair it is not meant to be used with, so most of the spend measures configurations that do not reflect Cairn as it is used.

A roster is declared before the set's first scored run with the same mandatory minimum as the rule-named option. That minimum is cairn yolo and cairn assess under models_strategy_1, the multi-prompt mirror of that yolo scenario, and manual_prompt under the most capable host model at its highest effort. Scenarios may be added to the roster while the set is in progress, but none is ever removed, and the set is complete once every scenario on the final roster is rated. The baseline guarantee holds, and a stronger manual pair or a new Cairn release that turns up mid-campaign can still join the set without starting a new one, which matters for a campaign that spans several days. Additions made after scores are visible bring back post-hoc selection. A configuration can be added because an early result looked promising, which biases best-of curve selection, and a set whose roster keeps growing may never count as complete. Whether a mid-set addition is allowed at all depends on how the comparison set is defined.

open-question.question: The benchmark's main branch is public, so the hidden requirements, the operator records, and every artifact are public and future models will train on them, wearing down the no-canned-solution requirement over time. How does the benchmark limit or account for its inputs and results leaking into training data?
open-question.recommendation: The only fully open option that keeps the hidden axis meaningful indefinitely: the canary and dated flag make erosion visible, and rotation is the stated response when it fires; current frontier cutoffs predate the draft, so the first sets run unflagged.
open-question.alternative: Everything stays public with the canary and the contamination flag as above. A flagged set, or inputs older than a stated age where no cutoff is published, triggers a rotation before the next headline comparison set. The rotation brings new hidden requirements with new seed evidence, and the prompts or the whole project change when the leak reaches the project's own rules. Only then is the old project retired, still public. It is the only fully open option that keeps the hidden axis meaningful indefinitely. Every retired input stays public and reproducible, while the scored inputs are always ones no model could have trained on. Every rotation is a seed and prompt bump that starts a new comparison set and breaks the trend's continuity. Each new hidden requirement needs its own calibration before scored runs, and authoring a project that meets every project requirement is recurring work. Its cost depends on how the trend continues across input changes and on what the hidden-requirement pilot procedure costs.

Everything stays public as the draft has it now: inputs, operator records, invocation outputs, run branches, snapshots, and ratings. Nothing is marked for exclusion, nothing is flagged, and nothing is rotated. The draft instead states leakage as a known limitation: a comparison set runs every scenario on the same models, so whatever a model has absorbed reaches every scenario of the set, and the hidden axis is expected to lose discriminating power as the inputs age. It costs nothing and keeps the design fully open and reproducible. Every artifact stays playable by URL, every input stays inspectable, and the limitation is stated honestly in the text rather than half-solved. The erosion does not hit all scenarios equally. A model that has seen "every question is about an animal" next to the zoo README can meet the hidden requirement without asking. That helps the manual deliveries most, because asking the operator is their only other route, so Cairn's measured hidden-axis gain shrinks silently and nothing tells a reader when it happened. The Closest Wins hidden requirements are also already stated in the public Cairn repository's draft, so the clock is already running.

Everything stays public. Every published file the benchmark writes (the inputs area, the records, the evaluation area, the README page, and the project section of the draft) carries one fixed benchmark canary string asking training pipelines to exclude it, following the BIG-bench convention. The seed is left unmarked so that no run sees the canary. There is no contamination accounting and no rotation. It is the cheapest real limiting measure and an established convention. Cooperating trainers can drop the content, and anyone can probe a model for the canary to test whether it trained on the benchmark, with no change to openness, publishing, or the run procedure. Exclusion depends on trainers honouring the string, and nothing stops copies that strip it. The draft and the gaps report are already public without it. The snapshots carry the seed README and the questions together, so an unmarked mirror of an artifact leaks the pairing anyway. The benchmark still has no way to tell a reader whether a given comparison set was run on a contaminated model.

Everything stays public with the canary string as in canary marking. In addition, each shared input records the date it was first published, the manifest or comparison-set definition records each model's vendor-stated training cutoff, and the analysis flags every comparison set where any model's cutoff falls after its inputs' first publication. The README page shows that flag beside the ranking table and the radar. Inputs are never rotated. It turns a silent erosion into a visible, dated property of each result. A reader can tell an uncontaminated comparison from a possibly contaminated one, and openness, playable artifacts, and trend continuity stay intact. Vendor cutoffs are approximate and sometimes unpublished, and a cutoff after publication shows only exposure, not use, so the flag is coarse in both directions. It records the damage without restoring discriminating power: once the frontier models postdate the inputs, every new set is flagged and the hidden axis means less with each one. How the flag interacts with set identity depends on which versions define a comparison set.

The statements the scoring rests on move to a separate private repository the harness reads. These are the hidden-requirement entries, the rating checklist's hidden lines, the operator definition, and the operator records and invocation outputs that quote its disclosures. The public main keeps the harness, the published snapshots, manifests stripped of operator content, the ratings without hidden-line evidence, and the aggregates. The draft in the Cairn repository describes the hidden requirement abstractly and stops naming it, and the current Closest Wins hidden requirements are replaced because they are already public. It removes the one thing whose leak most directly defeats the benchmark, the written statement of each hidden requirement and its check. It does that while keeping artifacts playable and most of the design inspectable. The published snapshots still leak the pairing. Each snapshot is the whole tree, seed README included, and every artifact that met the requirement shows the answer, so a model trained on enough snapshots can learn it without ever seeing the statement. External readers can no longer audit how the hidden axis was scored, and the benchmark now depends on a private repository the "one canonical repository" layout does not have.

The benchmark repository, its run branches, and its snapshots are private, and GitHub Pages publishes no artifacts. The only public output is the ranking table, the radar, and the trend, on a public page or in Cairn's changelog. The Cairn draft names no hidden requirement, and Closest Wins' current hidden requirements are replaced because the draft has already published them. It is the strongest limit available. Nothing scrapeable carries the inputs, the artifacts, or the records, so the no-canned-solution requirement and the hidden axis wear down only through deliberate disclosure. It gives up what the README page is built on: artifacts a reader can open and compare side by side as proof, and a record anyone can audit or re-run. The published scores become claims a reader must take on trust, which weakens them as evidence of whether Cairn helps, the benchmark's stated purpose.

The benchmark keeps two input sets. A public development set (the current project, prompts, and hidden requirements, fully published as now, artifacts included) serves the fast loop, ablations, and candidate commits. A private held-out set (its own prompts or hidden requirements, with its artifacts and records unpublished while live) is the only input behind the README page's ranking table and radar. When the held-out set is retired it is published in full and replaced by a fresh one. It keeps development fully open and reproducible while the headline comparison runs on inputs no model can have trained on, and retiring the held-out set publishes it eventually, so nothing stays secret for good. Every held-out set needs its own authoring and calibration, which doubles the input work. Headline artifacts are not playable and the headline cannot be audited externally while the set is live. Development results and headline results are on different inputs, so the fast loop no longer predicts the page directly. Each replacement is an input change whose trend continuity depends on how the trend continues across input changes.

open-question.question: Phase 1 is run for every scenario "as many times as the set calls for", with no number set and no stopping rule, so a margin between two scenarios can be noise. How many runs per scenario does a comparison set require?
open-question.recommendation: Three is the smallest count that gives a median and a range per cell, so one run off the rails cannot alone decide a rank, while a set stays within a solo maintainer's budget; it binds the roster's scenarios, and a development or ablation run outside the roster keeps the fast loop's single run.
open-question.alternative: The draft fixes the count at three phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child, so every row rests on three runs per prompt. The smallest count that yields a median and a range per score, so a spread can stand beside each cell and a run that went off the rails cannot alone decide a rank, at three times the cost of a single run. Three runs give only a rough spread: an interval from three points is wide, so most margins between close scenarios still come out unresolved, and a binary-heavy axis like hidden moves in thirds; what the spread is and how ties are called are the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions' to settle.

The draft fixes the count at one phase-1 run per scenario of a comparison set, for every scenario alike, with phase 2 run once from it as now; the runs column then always reads 1 and a margin is read as a single observation. Cheapest complete set: every scenario costs one chain per phase, the same unit as the development fast loop, so a full set (the Cairn chains being the costliest and likeliest to hit usage limits) stays affordable and finishes soonest. Gives no spread at all, so no margin between two scenarios can be told from noise and the hidden axis (two pass-or-fail checks per run) swings by a whole third of the overall score on one run; it resolves the gap only by stating that the page's ranking is anecdotal.

The draft fixes the count at five phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child. Enough runs for an interval narrow enough to separate a moderate margin, such as Cairn rows against the best manual row, while keeping a set within a few days of runs. Five times the single-run cost on every scenario, the Cairn chains and their usage-limit exposure included, and still too few to resolve small margins or to estimate the hidden axis finer than in fifths.

The draft fixes the count at ten phase-1 runs per scenario for every scenario of a comparison set, declared before the set's first scored run with no stopping rule, each with its own phase-2 child. Gives intervals tight enough that small margins and per-axis differences, the hidden axis included, can be read as findings rather than noise, which is what the page's claim that several Cairn rows stand above the best manual row needs. Ten full chains per phase per scenario make a set cost roughly ten times a single pass and take many days, which multiplies the infrastructure-failure and CLI-version drift a long campaign meets and puts the release gate's slow loop further out of reach.

The draft fixes a stopping rule instead of a number: every scenario starts with a declared minimum (three runs), and further phase-1 runs, each with its phase-2 child, are added to the scenarios whose margin to an adjacent ranked row is still unresolved until it resolves or a declared cap (such as ten) is reached; minimum, cap, and rule are declared before the set's first scored run, and scenarios may end with different run counts. Spends runs only where a margin is close, so clearly separated scenarios stay cheap and close ones get the resolution they need, with the stopping rule fixed in advance rather than left to the maintainer. Adaptive stopping inflates false separations unless the rule corrects for it, unequal counts complicate the table and when a set counts as complete, and the rule depends on how the spread is computed and what counts as a tie, which the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions own.

The draft fixes a uniform count for the scenarios that appear on the page (the four primary deliveries), declared before the set's first scored run and no fewer than three, with no stopping rule, while ablation deliveries and candidate-commit scenarios, which appear only in the analysis output, run once each. Concentrates the cost on the rows the published ranking and radar rest on, while the ablation and candidate runs stay at the fast loop's one-run price that the development uses already assume. Ablation and candidate comparisons inherit no spread, so a single-run result can still mislead a development decision, and the rule needs a stated boundary of which scenarios are primary, which depends on the roster the scenario-roster question owns.
