The draft fixes no number but requires every comparison set to declare its run count per scenario (uniform across the set's scenarios, at least two) in the set's definition before its first scored run, recorded beside the set's other versioned inputs, so later runs cannot be added after results are seen. Closes the stopping-rule hole, the count being fixed before any result can influence it, while leaving each set free to match its count to its budget and purpose. Different sets can carry different counts, so the trend across sets mixes rows of unequal precision, and the draft still says nothing about what count makes a margin meaningful; whether the declaration rides in the set's definition depends on the comparison-set-definition question.

The draft keeps "as many times as the set calls for" with no number and no stopping rule, the gap rejected with the reason stated in the text: the runs column already shows how many runs stand behind each row, and noise is left to whatever spread and tie handling the page reports. Commits no budget and no statistical design before a single run exists, so the first sets can be run at whatever count the maintainer can afford and the number chosen later from observed variance. Leaves optional stopping open, since runs can be added until a margin looks right, and a margin between two scenarios stays possibly noise unless the spread-reporting and tie-threshold questions supply what this count would have.

open-question.question: Each family's radar curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the best of several noisy scores is biased upward, more so for Cairn, which has many configurations (versions times strategies) where manual has few. Which scenario is each family's radar curve drawn from?
open-question.recommendation: Declaring each family's scenario before the first scored run removes the best-of-several bias outright and matches the Cairn curves and their mirror by construction, and with the roster's rule-named strongest manual pair as the manual reference the baseline is the a-priori strongest rather than a weak one.
open-question.alternative: Before a comparison set's first scored run, the set's definition names one reference scenario per family (for example both cairn deliveries for the current release under models_strategy_1, the multi-prompt control mirroring that yolo scenario, and one declared manual_prompt pair), and each curve is drawn from its declared scenario whatever the table's ranking turns out to be; every other configuration appears only in the table. Removes the selection bias outright, since nothing about the chart depends on which noisy score came out highest, and fixes the scenarios behind the curves so the two Cairn curves and the multi-prompt curve are matched by construction. The radar no longer shows any family at its best, so a declared manual pair that turns out weaker than another rated manual configuration makes the Cairn margin read against a weak baseline, exactly what the draft wanted to avoid; its worth depends on what the set must hold and how it is declared, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

Each family's curve stays drawn from its highest-ranked scenario in the current comparison set's table, as the draft has it, and the gap is rejected in the draft's text with the reason stated: the ranking table lists every rated configuration, so the radar is read as best against best and the table carries the configuration count. Needs no new rule, no extra declaration, and no change to the analysis, and it keeps the draft's reading of every approach at its best configuration and of every radar value as a ranking-table cell. The upward bias of a best-of-several pick stays in the chart and grows with the number of configurations, which favours the Cairn families (and the multi-prompt controls that mirror them) over manual_prompt, so the page's claim of a fair, honest margin rests on a selection known to favour the system it measures.

Each family's curve stays drawn from its highest-ranked scenario, and the line under the chart that names each curve's scenario also states how many rated configurations it was chosen from, with one sentence in the radar text saying that a best-of pick is biased upward the more configurations stand behind it; the draft's sentence calling the selection fair is rewritten to match. Keeps the draft's selection and every radar value a table cell while removing the unstated part of the bias, so a reader can weigh a Cairn curve chosen from many configurations against a manual one chosen from few. Discloses the bias without reducing it: the curves still overstate the many-configuration families, and the chart, which a reader takes in before the line under it, keeps showing a margin the disclosure itself says is inflated.

One Cairn configuration (a version under a model strategy) is chosen as the one whose cairn scenarios rank highest in the set, and the cairn yolo, cairn assess, and multi-prompt curves are all drawn from that one configuration's three scenarios; the manual_prompt curve is drawn from its own highest-ranked scenario. Makes the gap between the two Cairn curves isolate the stakeholder's turn and the gap to the multi-prompt curve isolate Cairn's structure, as the draft's radar text claims they do, which independent best-of picks across different versions and strategies cannot guarantee, and it replaces three best-of selections over the Cairn configurations with one. Still selects on the same noisy scores it then draws, so the Cairn curves keep an upward bias that grows with the number of configurations, and the multi-prompt curve is no longer that family's best, which can understate the strongest manual-side configuration the draft says Cairn is read against.

The two Cairn curves are drawn from pre-declared reference scenarios named before the set's first scored run (one version under one model strategy), while the manual_prompt and multi-prompt curves are each drawn from their family's highest-ranked scenario in the table. Turns the selection bias against Cairn rather than for it: the Cairn curves carry no best-of inflation while the manual curves keep theirs, so any Cairn margin the chart shows is conservative and the draft's reading against the strongest manual configuration still holds. Mixes two selection rules on one chart, so the gap between curves no longer measures any single comparison, the multi-prompt curve may come from a different configuration than the Cairn curves it is meant to mirror, and a real Cairn margin can be understated or hidden.

Each family's curve is drawn from its highest-ranked scenario among an equal number of configurations per family, the same count for every family and the configurations in each pool declared before the set's first scored run; a family with more rated configurations than the count draws only from its declared pool. Keeps every family shown at its best and every radar value a table cell while making the best-of bias the same size for every family, so it no longer favours the family with more configurations. Equal bias is not zero bias, so every curve stays inflated relative to a single scenario's true score, and the manual_prompt family must be run under as many strategies as Cairn has configurations in its pool, raising the cost of every set; its viability depends on what the set's roster must hold, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

Each family's scenario is still chosen as its highest-ranked, but the ranking used for the choice is computed from one fixed half of each scenario's runs (declared before the set, for example the odd-numbered runs) and the curve's values from the other half, so the chosen scenario's drawn scores come from runs that played no part in choosing it. Keeps every family shown at its best configuration while removing the selection bias from the drawn values for every family alike, whatever the number of configurations behind it. Halves the runs behind every drawn value, making each curve noisier, and the drawn values are no longer cells of the ranking table unless the table gains held-out columns, against the draft's rule that nothing depends on the chart; it needs at least two runs per scenario, a count the runs-per-scenario question owns.

No single scenario is chosen: each family's curve is the per-axis mean over every rated scenario of that family in the current comparison set (for the Cairn families, the current version's scenarios across its model strategies), and the line under the chart states how many scenarios each curve averages. Involves no selection at all, so there is no best-of bias, and it matches the ranking table's own stated reading that Cairn wins as a family of configurations rather than as one tuned winner. A curve is no longer any scenario a reader could run, its values are not table cells, and a weak or deliberately exploratory configuration drags its family down, so the curve's height depends on which configurations happened to be rated, an axis the scenario-roster question owns.

open-question.question: The ranking table has a runs column but no spread or interval beside any score, so a reader cannot tell a margin between two scenarios from noise. Is a per-run spread or interval reported beside every score, and where?
open-question.recommendation: A min-to-max range is honest at three runs where an interval is wide or degenerate, needs no distributional assumption, and sits in the cell a reader already compares; cost and time stay means since the report raised noise on quality only.
open-question.alternative: Each score cell of the README ranking table (overall, the three axes, and the lost count) carries the minimum and maximum over the scenario's runs beside its mean, written in the cell as, for example, 82 (76–88), each run counted as one phase-1 run with its phase-2 child, whose two prompt scores are averaged as the scenario mean is; the analysis output carries the same ranges and every run's individual scores. Cost, time, invocations, and sessions stay means without spread, and the radar draws means only. A descriptive range needs no distributional assumption, is honest at any run count of two or more, and puts the variability on the landing page in the same cell a reader is already comparing, with no new column. A range says how far runs scattered, not whether two means differ, so overlapping ranges are read as a tie by eye with no stated rule, and the range widens with every added run; a row resting on one run shows no range at all, which depends on the run count the runs-per-scenario sibling sets.

No spread or interval is reported anywhere: the ranking table keeps its runs column as the only sign of how many runs stand behind a row, the analysis output carries means only, and the radar draws means only. The draft states that a margin between two rows carries no measure of its noise, and leaves handling noise, if at all, to how many runs a set requires and to how the rank treats near-equal scores. Keeps the table at its twelve columns and the analysis at one number per cell, and adds no statistic whose meaning at a small run count would itself need explaining. Leaves the gap exactly as the report found it: a reader still cannot tell a margin from noise, and the page's headline reading (several Cairn rows above the best manual row) rests on means of unstated variability; whether that is tolerable depends on the axes the runs-per-scenario and rank-tie siblings settle.

As the range option, the minimum and maximum over the scenario's runs written in the cell beside each mean, but on every numeric cell of the README ranking table: the overall, the three axes, and the lost count, and also cost in dollars, wall-clock time, and attentive sessions; invocations made over planned stays as it is, and the radar draws means only. The analysis output carries the same ranges and every run's individual values. Puts cost and time under the same scrutiny as quality, so the page's rule that a quality win is read beside its cost holds for the cost's variability too, which matters most for Cairn, whose long chains are where a runaway or retried run inflates one run's cost. Every cell of an already twelve-column table doubles in width, and the cost spread answers a question the report did not raise; it shares the range option's limits, a range that is not a test and empty at one run, the latter depending on the runs-per-scenario sibling.

Each score cell of the README ranking table (overall, the three axes, and the lost count) carries a 95% confidence interval on its mean beside the mean, computed over the scenario's runs (each a phase-1 run with its phase-2 child), by a method the draft names once (a bootstrap over runs or a t-interval); the analysis output carries the same intervals and every run's individual scores. Cost and time stay means, and the radar draws means only. An interval on the mean speaks to the question the reader actually has, how precisely each row's score is known, and two rows whose intervals do not overlap differ by more than noise under a conservative reading. At the small run counts an expensive Cairn chain affords, a t-interval is very wide and a bootstrap over a handful of runs is unstable or degenerate, so the method and a minimum run count must be stated, which ties this option to the runs-per-scenario sibling; overlapping per-row intervals also understate significance compared with an interval on the difference.

The per-score premise is rejected: instead of a spread beside each score, the README ranking table gains one column holding, for every row, the difference between its overall score and the overall of a stated reference row (the best manual row) with a 95% interval on that difference over the two scenarios' runs; the per-axis differences with their intervals, and every run's individual scores, go in the analysis output. The score cells and the radar stay means. Answers exactly the comparison the page exists to make, whether a Cairn row stands above the best manual row by more than noise, in one column, with a single interval per row that is tighter and more honest than reading two per-row intervals for overlap. The whole results section carries one consistent, explicitly falsifiable hypothesis, the same framing the phase-2 paragraph uses. It rewrites the most prose, including radar text beside the curve-selection reasoning a sibling question may also change (a condition on that radar curve choice). The opening sentence of "The ranking table" in ideas/benchmark_for_cairn.md stays as written ("The table shows that Cairn beats the other approaches as a family of configurations, not as one tuned winner"). The opening sentence is removed rather than reworded, and the table section opens with what the table is: one row per rated configuration of the four primary deliveries, ordered by rank. open-question.question: The rank orders scenarios by overall score and breaks ties by cost, with no threshold below which two scores count as equal, so a difference within noise still orders two rows. Is there a margin under which two overall scores tie and cost decides?
open-question.recommendation: Rows are ordered only where the set's own per-run ranges separate them and tied rows share a rank, so the headline reading is claimed only when the data supports it, no constant has to be argued for, and cost stays unranked as the draft states.
open-question.alternative: The margin is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise, by a declared statistical bound on the difference of two scenarios' per-run overall scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported); scenarios within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank. The most defensible statement the page can make: rows are ordered only where the set's own data separates them, and the benchmark never weighs cost against quality for the reader. Depends on several runs per scenario and a computed spread, owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions; it carries the most analysis machinery, the threshold varies between comparison sets, and with few runs most rows may tie, leaving the table's headline reading and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" (the Radar curve selection question) without a clear order.

The rank stays as the draft has it: scenarios are ordered by the exact overall score, only two exactly equal scores tie, and cost breaks such a tie in favour of the cheaper scenario. No margin is declared, and whether a margin between two rows is noise is left to whatever the table reports beside the scores. Nothing new to define, justify, or keep in step: the rank is a total order computed mechanically from the per-axis means, with no constant anyone has to argue for and no grouping rule for chains of near-equal scores. Overall scores are means of fractions, so exact equality practically never occurs and the cost rule is dead text; a difference well inside noise still orders two rows, so the table's intended reading (Cairn rows above the best manual row) can rest on noise, and a reader can tell otherwise only if the table reports a spread, which the Score spread reporting question owns.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them (for example whole points on the 0 to 100 scale): two scores that print the same tie, and the cheaper scenario ranks higher. No noise-based margin is declared. The rank never contradicts what the reader sees, since two rows showing the same overall are never ordered by an invisible decimal, and the existing cost rule becomes live without introducing a tuned constant. Print precision is a formatting choice, not a noise estimate: differences of a few points, which can still be rater or run noise, keep ordering rows, so the gap the question raises is narrowed only at its smallest end.

Overall scores are compared at the precision the table prints them: two scores that print the same share one rank number and are marked as tied, and their listing order within the tie carries no claim (cost no longer breaks ties). No noise-based margin is declared. Removes the contradiction between the draft's rule that cost is never ranked and its use of cost as a tie-breaker, while keeping the rank consistent with what is printed and adding no constant. Like the other print-precision option it leaves noise-sized differences ordering rows; and a shared top rank within a family leaves the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" ambiguous, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; two scenarios whose overall scores differ by less than it tie, and the cheaper one ranks higher. Tie groups are formed from the top of the order down, each row joining the group whose top row it is within the margin of, so chains of near-equal scores resolve one way. A quality difference too small to trust can no longer put an expensive scenario above a cheaper one, which is the reading the cost tie-break was written for; the rule is simple, reproducible from the columns, and identical across comparison sets, so ranks under it compare over the trend. The margin's value is chosen before any noise has been measured, so it is a guess that may be too tight to matter or too loose to separate real differences; it brings cost into the rank, against the draft's statement that cost is never ranked, and can lift a cheap manual row above a Cairn row on the page's headline reading.

The draft declares one fixed margin in points on the 0 to 100 overall score, set before a comparison set's first scored run and versioned with the analysis; scenarios whose overall scores fall within it of their group's top row share one rank number and are marked as tied, and cost plays no part in the rank, staying a column the reader weighs. Says exactly what the data supports, that the tied rows are indistinguishable on quality, without the benchmark weighing cost for the reader, which keeps the rank consistent with the draft's rule that cost is never ranked. The margin is still a guess made before noise is measured; tied groups make the table's ordering partly uninformative, and the radar's "highest-ranked scenario" becomes ambiguous within a tied group, which needs a rule from the Radar curve selection question.

The margin is not a constant but is derived per comparison set from the set's own measured noise: two scenarios tie when the difference between their overall scores lies within a declared statistical bound computed from their per-run scores (for example overlapping intervals at a declared level, widened by the rater agreement figure where one is reported), and within a tie the cheaper scenario ranks higher. The bound's formula and level are declared in the draft before the first scored run. A tie means precisely "this difference is within the noise the set actually showed", so the rank tracks the data rather than a guessed constant, and cost decides only where quality genuinely cannot. It exists only if the set carries several runs per scenario and computes a per-run spread, axes owned by the Runs per scenario and Score spread reporting questions (with one run per scenario no bound can be computed); the analysis grows more complex, the threshold moves between comparison sets so ranks are not formed under one rule over the trend, and cost enters the rank against the draft's statement that it is never ranked.

open-question.question: The hidden-requirements axis rests on two checks per run (one reading line in phase 1 and one test line in phase 2) yet weighs one third of the overall score, as much as roughly thirty-seven implied lines. Does the hidden axis keep equal weight in the overall score, or is it reported beside an overall computed without it?
open-question.recommendation: The hidden axis is the outcome the benchmark exists to test, so it keeps full influence on the rank, with the per-axis columns and ranges beside the overall and the measured tie rule absorbing the two-check noise as ties rather than a weight burying the signal.
open-question.alternative: The overall score stays the unweighted mean of the stated, hidden, and implied axes, and the rank still orders by it. The hidden requirement stays one per prompt, so the axis keeps resting on the phase-1 reading line (a count out of ten) and the phase-2 yes-or-no test line. The draft adds the reason the hidden axis keeps its third despite its two checks, and the ranking table keeps the per-axis columns beside the overall as it does now. It keeps the draft's stated rule that equal weights are the only weights nobody has to argue for, and leaves the axis the question-and-answer loop is tested on at full influence on the rank, where the draft expects Cairn's gain to show. Two checks per run carry as much of the overall as about thirty-seven implied lines, and the phase-2 check is binary, so one run's 0 or 100 on a single test moves the overall by a third of the scale and can reorder the rank on noise; the draft would be keeping, knowingly, the imbalance the design-gaps report raised.

The overall score becomes the unweighted mean of the stated and implied axes only, and the rank orders by that. The hidden axis stays a scored axis in every other place: its own ranking-table column beside the overall, and its axis on the radar. The draft states why the hidden axis is reported beside the rank rather than in it. The rank no longer swings on two checks, and the hidden result is still shown on its own, unblended, where a reader sees the clearest evidence the benchmark produces without it being diluted or amplified by a weighting choice. The one axis designed to show what Cairn's question loop buys stops affecting the rank, so a scenario that never meets a hidden requirement can rank first, and the headline ordering no longer reflects the outcome the benchmark exists to test; a reader must read two numbers to see the comparison the draft frames as its point.

The hidden axis stays in the overall score but at a declared weight below the other two (for example half the weight of each), the overall becoming a weighted mean whose weights the draft states and fixes per comparison set. The hidden column and radar axis stay as they are. The hidden result still bears on the rank, so a scenario that surfaces the hidden requirement is rewarded, while one noisy binary check can no longer move the overall by a full third of the scale. Any weight below a third and above zero is a number someone has to argue for, the very thing the draft's equal-weight rule avoids, and the chosen value is arbitrary with no line-count or evidential basis to anchor it; a later change to it is an analysis version that splits comparisons made before and after it.

The overall score stops being a mean of axis scores and becomes the passing share of every checklist line pooled across axes, each line counting once (a reading line contributing its items' fraction), so each axis weighs in proportion to how many lines it has: the hidden axis about two lines' worth across both prompts, the stated axis its sentences, and the implied axis its roughly thirty-seven lines. The per-axis scores stay in their columns and on the radar. The weights follow mechanically from the checklist with nothing chosen by hand, so each check counts the same and the overall's sensitivity to any one check matches the evidence behind it. It also reweights the stated axis, which the draft calls the floor under the others, down to a handful of lines against the implied list, so the overall becomes mostly an implied-coverage score; the hidden result all but vanishes from the rank, and every later change to an implied list's length silently shifts every axis's weight.

Equal weight is kept, and the premise that the axis rests on two checks is rejected instead: the "one per prompt" rule is replaced by a fixed number of hidden requirements per prompt (several, each with its own seed evidence and check line), so the hidden axis becomes the mean over several checks per prompt like the other axes. It removes the imbalance at its cause rather than by weighting: the axis that tests the question loop keeps its third of the rank while resting on enough checks that one missed requirement no longer swings it. Each extra hidden requirement needs seed evidence calibrated so the prompt gives no reason to ask yet the question settles it, in a small seed README where several planted pieces of evidence can point at each other or at an implied convention; it multiplies the authoring and calibration work, changes the seed and the Closest Wins project section, and depends on whatever calibration procedure the hidden-requirement pilot sets.

The overall score and the rank are dropped: the ranking table shows the three axis scores side by side with no blended number, ordered by a fixed key the draft states (such as delivery family then scenario id), and the radar stays the per-axis comparison. No weight for the hidden axis, or any axis, is set because no axes are combined. No weighting question exists at all, so nothing about the hidden axis's two checks is amplified or buried, and the page shows only numbers each re-derivable from the checklist lines, consistent with the draft's refusal to weigh trade-offs for the reader. The page loses its one-glance answer to which approach is best and the table's reason to order its rows, and the radar's per-family curve is currently chosen by rank, so this depends on how the radar curve selection is settled; the tie-by-cost rule and the "several Cairn rows above the best manual row" reading lose their basis.
